en: Sutta Nipāta 5.19 Pārāyanānugītigāthā “I shall sing the sequel to the Pārāyana.”
(Thus spoke the venerable Piṅgiya:
"Just as he saw it, so he declared it;
stainless and of vast wisdom,"
The elephant who is free from desire and free from craving—
why would he speak falsehood? For one whose stains and delusion have been abandoned, [how could there be lying]?
Having abandoned conceit and malice—
I shall now proclaim his praise,
with words endowed with beauty.
The Buddha, the dispeller of darkness, the all-seeing,
who has gone to the end of the world and transcended all states of existence,
is free from taints and has abandoned all suffering.
The one called Truth, O Brahmā, has been attended by me.
Just as a bird, having abandoned a small grove, would dwell in a forest abounding in fruit; so have I come to you.
Thus, having abandoned those who see little,
I have reached the great ocean like a swan.
Those who previously prophesied for me—
"Alas, from the teaching of Gotama!
'It was thus,' 'it will be thus'—
all that is merely hearsay."
All that merely increases speculative reasoning.
He alone is the dispeller of darkness,
the radiant one, the maker of light.
Gotama is one of vast wisdom,
Gotama is one of vast intelligence—
he who taught the Dhamma to me.
Visible here and now, timeless,
the destruction of craving, free from calamity—
for which there is no comparison anywhere.
“Why indeed do you dwell apart from them even for a moment, O Piṅgiya?
From the Gotamas of vast wisdom, [you should not depart].”
O Gotamas of vast intelligence!
He who taught you the Dhamma— visible here and now and not subject to time— [is the Blessed One].
The destruction of craving, free from danger,
for which there is no comparison anywhere—
I do not dwell apart from that.
Even for a moment, O Brahmin,
are the Gotamas of vast wisdom,
the Gotamas of immense intelligence.
He who taught me the Dhamma—
visible here and now, timeless,
the destruction of craving, free from affliction—
For whom there is no likeness anywhere—
I behold him with the mind as if with the eye,
O Brahmin, day and night, being heedful.
Paying homage, I pass the night;
by that alone, I consider it no absence [from the Teacher].
Faith, joy, mind, and mindfulness—
I do not depart from the teaching of Gotama;
to whichever direction the one of vast wisdom goes,
I am bowed down before him in that very place.
I am old and my strength is feeble;
for that reason, my body does not go there on its own.
Yet, by forming the intention, I always go.
For my mind, O Brahmin, was intent upon that.
Lying in the mire and struggling,
I drifted from island to island.
Then I saw the Fully Enlightened One,
who has crossed the flood and is free from taints.
"Just as it was with Vakkali, whose faith was liberated..."
Bhadrāvudha and Āḷavika Gotama; even so,
you too shall release your faith, for you,
Piṅgiya, will go to the further shore of the realm of death.
“Having heard the words of the Sage, I have even greater confidence:
the Perfectly Awakened One has pulled back the veil.”
He was entirely possessed of inspired eloquence;
having directly known the higher deities,
he understood everything, both the superior and the inferior.
The Teacher who brings an end to questions for those who declare themselves free from doubt—
unshakable and unassailable.
“For whom there is no comparison anywhere:
‘I shall certainly go; I have no doubt in this matter’—know me thus as one whose mind is resolutely intent.”
The fifth chapter: Pārāyaṇa.
The summary of the suttas:
Uraga and Dhaniya, and...
The Rhinoceros Horn, and Agriculture;
Cunda, and Existence once more,
the Outcaste, and What Should Be Done.
Then the yakkha Hemavata [recited] the Vijayasutta and the Munisuttavara.
This is the first section on the forest-dwellers; it is the excellent chapter.
One who has mastered the twelve suttas and is well-distinguished;
this excellent chapter, "The Snake," taught by the Visionary One,
the Stainless One, shines forth clearly.
Ratanāmagandha, Hirimaṅgalanāma,
Suciloma, Kapila, and Brāhmaṇadhamma;
Nāvā, Kiṁsīla, and Uṭṭhāna.
And furthermore, there is the Rāhulovāda and the Vaṅgīsa;
here also is the Sammāparibbājanīya and the excellently analyzed Dhammika-sutta.
In the second [varga], he was called the foremost of the Cūḷakavagga,
a bearer of fourteen suttas; his name was Pabbajjapadhānasubhāsita.
Pūraḷāsa, and again Māgha;
Sabhiya, Keṇiya, and the one named Salla,
the excellent Vāseṭṭha, and Kālika as well.
The excellent Nālaka Sutta is well-expounded;
contemplating it thus once more,
he was the bearer of twelve suttas in the third [watch].
The excellent Vagga is Mahānāma;
the excellent Kāmaguha is Duṭṭhaka by name;
the excellent Suddha is Paramaṭṭhaka by name.
Jarā, Mettiyavara, Suvibhatta,
Pasūra, Māgaṇḍiya, Purābheda,
Kalaha, Vivāda, and Ubhato-viyūha.
Tuvaṭaka, Attadaṇḍa, and Sāriputta;
he who held sixteen suttas in the fourth [section] is called the excellent Aṭṭhakavagga.
In the delightful kingdom of Magadha,
in that excellent region where those who have performed merit dwell,
lies the most beautifully arranged and noble Pāsāṇaka Cetiya.
The Blessed One, the best of the assembly,
dwelt there while both groups,
from a distance of twelve yojanas, were gathered together.
It is said that when questioned by the sixteen brahmins,
he elucidated the Dhamma and gave it as a gift in response to their sixteen questions.
The Jina, the foremost of bipeds, for the welfare of the world,
taught the Dhamma which clarifies the meaning,
is full of beautiful phrasing, and produces supreme security.
The Best of Bipeds taught this excellent discourse,
which is variegated with many teachings and is the cause for liberation from all defilements.
The phrasing is connected with the meaning of the words,
expressed through syllables, analogies, and profundity;
it is shattered by the wisdom that investigates the world.
The Best of Bipeds, the Foremost of Men, taught this supreme Sutta:
"Stainless and pure amidst the stain of lust;
stainless and pure amidst the stain of hatred."
The Best of Bipeds taught this excellent discourse,
which is free from delusion, stainless, and pure in its summit,
having shattered the light of knowledge that investigates the world.
Stainless amidst the stains of the defilements,
pure amidst the impurities of misconduct,
and having shattered the light of worldly deliberation—
The Best of Men, the Foremost of Bipeds, taught this excellent discourse on the outflows, the bonds, the yokes,
the afflictions, the hindrances, and the three stains.
For the sake of his liberation from defilements,
the Best of Bipeds taught this excellent discourse,
which dispels all stainless defilements.
The Best of Bipeds taught this supreme discourse: passionless, dispassionate, immovable, sorrowless,
peaceful, sublime, and a Dhamma exceedingly difficult to see.
He who has destroyed passion, hatred, and pride, who is at peace,

and who has transcended the womb, the four states of existence, the five destinies, and the fivefold consciousness; he who has escaped from the creeper of craving, which is the covering and shelter of delight— [to him I pay homage].
The Best of Bipeds, the Teacher, taught this supreme sutta—
profound, difficult to see, subtle, and skillful;
to be understood by the wise, its meaning is refined.
The Best of Bipeds taught this excellent discourse,
which shatters with the knowledge that investigates the world;
it is like a garland of flowers made of the ninefold [scriptures] worn upon the neck.
The Best of Bipeds taught this excellent discourse,
which analyzes the faculties, jhānas, and liberations,
and which upholds the noble vehicle of the Eightfold Path.
Like the moon, stainless and utterly pure;
like the ocean, a jewel-mind of supreme beauty;
like a flower, with splendor like the sun.
The Best of Bipeds, the Teacher, taught this supreme Sutta—
secure, auspicious, blissfully cool, and peaceful;
the ultimate goal, the supreme refuge from death.
For the sake of one who had seen perfect peace,
the Best of Bipeds taught this excellent discourse.
The Sutta Nipāta Pāḷi is complete.
